first_impression.reaction: Three short paragraphs, then Key Takeaways straight after. On the train that's fine. The myth-busting angle is a bit different from the usual listicle, so I kept going. But the takeaways tell me about myths and destination weddings, not 'here are the main traditions', which is what I actually typed.

journey.quote: Ask, and you will usually hear a story: a vein that runs to the heart, bridesmaids dressed to confuse evil spirits, a month of honey wine. Some of these are history. Many are not.
journey.reaction: Okay, that's a hook. I've heard the vein thing. Now I want to know which ones are fake.

journey.quote: Many popular origin stories, including the "vein of love" and the month of mead behind "honeymoon", are not supported by the documented record.
journey.reaction: Quick, specific, useful. This is what I wanted the takeaways to do.

journey.quote: At a destination wedding, rituals such as handfasting, a quaich or personal vows sit well in a symbolic ceremony, while the legal paperwork needs to be valid where you marry.
journey.reaction: I didn't search for destination weddings. Fine if it's one line, but two of the four takeaways lean that way. I just wanted the list of traditions.

journey.section: Rings on the fourth finger of the left hand
journey.quote: Britannica records that a few sources suggest ancient cultures believed this, and that modern medicine has shown there is no such vein.
journey.reaction: Love that it names the source. I'd actually repeat this to friends.

journey.quote: The white dress is a 186-year-old fashion that became tradition.
journey.reaction: Good, punchy, and it's clearly up to date. Answers my 'is this still true' itch.

journey.section: How to choose which traditions to keep
journey.quote: Here is how we would weigh the traditions in this guide for a destination wedding. It is our editorial view, not a rule.
journey.reaction: This table is the thing I'd screenshot. Why is it right at the bottom? On my phone I'd never have scrolled this far without the jump.

journey.quote: Something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue; some versions add a sixpence in the shoe. Anyone in the couple can carry them.
journey.reaction: Fast, direct answer. Exactly how an FAQ should read.

journey.section: Local wedding traditions you can borrow at your destination
journey.quote: For a wider tour, see our round-up of unusual wedding traditions around the world.
journey.reaction: If I'm curious this is the link I'd tap next. Good.

unanswered_questions: Is there a quick list near the top of the traditions this page covers, so I can jump to the one I care about?
When was this page last updated?

turn_offs_found.why: The scannable summary I'd want first sits near the very end of a very long page. On a phone that's a lot of scrolling to reach the most useful bit.

turn_offs_found.quote: This guide sets out where each tradition really comes from, using museum, encyclopaedia and church sources, and flags the stories that do not hold up.
turn_offs_found.why: Not a big deal, but it's a third intro paragraph describing the article instead of answering. One short line would do.

would_share_with: A friend who's engaged and keeps quoting the vein of love thing
Group chat, as a screenshot of the keep/adapt/skip table

cta_reaction.quote: Through Wonderland Concierge, one Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, start to finish.
cta_reaction.why: I came for a quick answer, I'm not planning anything yet. It didn't annoy me, it's one line and not a pop-up. I might bookmark the page, but I'm not enquiring today.

top_3_changes: Put the keep/adapt/skip table (or a short jump list of the traditions covered) right after Key Takeaways so phone readers get the overview first.
Make one Key Takeaway a plain answer to the search, e.g. the main traditions in one line, and keep destination framing to a single bullet.
Show a visible 'last updated' date near the top so I know it's current.
